claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is controlled primarily by a continuous chromium-enriched passive oxide layer.
The protective passive layer consists primarily of Cr2O3.
The chromium-rich oxide self-heals after damage and impedes ingress of aggressive species.
High-alloy stainless steels containing at least 12 wt% Cr have a homogeneous distribution of chromium in the as-polished matrix.
A surface heat treatment or controlled anneal promotes chromium diffusion to the surface and produces a uniform, adherent Cr2O3 film.
Mechanical polishing removes pre-existing oxide heterogeneities.
The passive film is chromium-enriched relative to the bulk steel.
A thin, continuous Cr2O3 film acts as a barrier to oxygen and corrosive ions.
The chromium-rich film rapidly reforms where it has been disrupted.
Under oxidizing conditions, chromium atoms preferentially diffuse from the steel surface and form a dense Cr2O3 layer.
The chemical stability and adhesion of the Cr2O3 layer limit oxygen and ion penetration.
Chromium in the substrate serves as a reservoir for rapid re-oxidation after local film damage.
Optimally heat-treated steels will exhibit higher oxide-film impedance than untreated or low-chromium steels.
Optimally heat-treated steels will exhibit lower anodic current density and lower mass loss than untreated or low-chromium steels.
After deliberate film disruption, treated steels will reform the passive film more rapidly than steels with insufficient chromium or unoptimized microstructures.
Steels containing less than 12 wt% Cr typically form nonuniform or nonprotective oxides and show greater corrosion current, mass loss, and pitting.
The proposed mechanism is limited to chromium-sufficient, microstructurally homogeneous steels in oxidizing aqueous environments at 25–100 °C.
Very high chloride concentrations or severe irradiation may compromise passive-film formation.
Corrosion behavior can be compared by varying chromium content and measuring electrochemical response in a controlled chloride solution.
